summary: Orion Trailhead is a Marswalk planner built around the ancient river delta in Jezero Crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover has been exploring since 2021. You can look around the area on an interactive map, follow a route that connects four locations, and see how a walk for two astronauts would work out. The map has several layers of NASA imagery, plus science stops and illustrative hazard zones. If you change the walking speed, the journey time and the total EVA time update straight away. It also has a radiation estimate and a checklist for the crew. We wanted to show how real NASA data can help people think about what future human missions to Mars might involve.
details:
Orion Trailhead is an interactive planner for a walk on Mars. It is based on the ancient river delta in Jezero Crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover has been exploring since it landed in 2021. We built it so people can look around the area and plan a trip for two astronauts.

The site is built around an interactive map made with Leaflet, using imagery from NASA Mars Trek. You can switch between optical (Viking), topography (Mars Global Surveyor MOLA), thermal (Mars Odyssey THEMIS), CTX and HiRISE (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter) layers to see the area at different scales and in different kinds of data. The route starts at a rover base and passes through three science stops: Brac Outcrop, Delta Front and Three Forks Sample Depot. Each stop has a marker and a popup with its science goal, a description of the terrain, a real Perseverance photo and links to NASA's pages.

There is also a planning panel. It works out the route distance, the walking time, the time spent at each stop and the total EVA time. You can change the walking speed and watch the numbers change. It also shows a rough radiation estimate, checks whether the route goes through any hazard zone, and has a checklist for the crew and equipment.

We didn't want this to be just a page of Mars photos. Putting real imagery, a route and some simple planning calculations together lets people think about what astronauts would have to deal with on the surface. We hope it makes planetary data easier to explore and shows how maps can help plan future human missions.

We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Leaflet 1.9.4 handles the map, NASA Mars Trek WMTS services supply the imagery, and the photos come from NASA's Mars 2020 image resources. It is hosted on Netlify and uses the Archivo and Space Mono fonts. We didn't use any extra hardware. Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS. The radiation estimate is based on the Mars surface average of about 0.67 millisieverts per day measured by NASA's Curiosity rover RAD instrument.

We tried to fit several features onto one screen: a map that can switch between black-and-white and real colours, a HUD mode that looks like a helmet display, a coordinate readout, a popup for each stop and the crew checklist. The code measures distances using Mars' radius, works out the time budget, and checks whether the route crosses any of the marked hazard areas.

While building it we thought about the terrain, the length of the route, walking speed, how long each stop would take, how two astronauts would work together, and what hazards they might meet. We were also careful about what our data can and can't tell us. The hazard zones are illustrative and haven't been checked as real safety boundaries. The radiation and time figures are simple estimates, not live measurements or certified predictions.

Use of Super Intelligence: ChatGPT and Claude assisted with code debugging, troubleshooting and improving explanatory text. The team reviewed and adapted suggestions during development.
